hero.title: Kolabr vs Slack
hero.lede: Everything you use Slack for, and the part Slack leaves to other tools: requests with an owner and a deadline your client can see, a wiki in every channel, and meetings and scheduled events tied to the work. Your clients join free, in as many channels as the work needs.

summary.title: What you get on top of chat
summary.body: Chat, threads, calls and files, as you have in Slack. Then requests with owners, categories and response targets, a wiki in every channel, playbooks for repeat work and scheduled events, in one subscription instead of three.

summary.title: The number that decides it
summary.body: Twelve people and eight clients with five people each, every client in more than one channel: $120 a month on Kolabr Pro, $455 on Slack Pro.* Slack bills those forty guests as members. Kolabr does not bill them at all.
summary.note: * Monthly terms on both. On annual terms it is $102 against $377. Slack prices checked 5 October 2026.

valueBand.title: What you get that Slack leaves to other tools
valueBand.lede: All of these are on Kolabr Pro, the plan the calculator below prices. None of them needs an app, an integration or another subscription.

items.title: Requests with an owner and a clock
items.body: Any message becomes a numbered request with a category, an owner and a response target, and routing sends it to the right person.
items.slack: Slack Lists track items with an assignee and a due date, in a list you design and keep current. There are no response targets.

items.title: The client sees the status
items.body: Guests see the owner, the status and the time left on the requests they are part of, so nobody has to ask for an update.
items.slack: A guest can see a List you share with them, as long as someone keeps it up to date.

items.title: A wiki in every channel
items.body: Articles with version history, readable by your guests, and suggested to a client while they are raising a request.
items.slack: Canvases: documents you can pin to a channel.

items.title: Meetings tied to the work
items.body: Video calls and scheduled events live in the channel and link to the request they are about, so the decision and the date stay with the work.
items.slack: Huddles give you calls in any channel. Dates come from a calendar app.

items.title: Playbooks for repeat work
items.body: Onboarding, an access request, a monthly close: deploy a playbook and the steps, owners and due dates are filled in for you.
items.slack: Workflow Builder automates steps you design and maintain.

items.title: Clients free in every channel
items.body: A guest needs an email address. They are free in as many channels as the work needs, with nothing to count and nothing that turns them into a paid account later.
items.slack: Free in one channel, up to five per paid member. A second channel bills them as a full member.

statement.title: The second channel is where it gets expensive
paragraphs: Slack gives you free guests on two conditions. Each one may be in a single channel, and you may have no more than five of them for every paid member. A client with a project channel, a billing question and a support thread is in three channels, so Slack bills them at the full member rate. A growing client list meets the second condition too: past five guests per member, every extra guest needs a paid account.
Kolabr has one kind of guest. Free, in as many channels as the work needs, with no allowance to track. The calculator below shows what that difference comes to for your own numbers.

image.alt: A Kolabr client channel: the agency team and the client's brand and legal people in the same conversation, with a pinned scope note and a request raised from a message

cost.title: What each one actually costs you
paragraphs: Per person the two are close: Kolabr Pro is $10 a month and Slack Pro $8.75, or $8.50 and $7.25 on annual terms. What decides the bill is your guests. On Slack, a client in more than one channel is billed as a full member, and one-channel guests are free only up to five per paid member.

What decides the value is everything beyond chat. Kolabr's price includes requests with response targets, a wiki in every channel, playbooks and scheduled events. On Slack you build those from Lists, canvases and workflows, or pay for another tool.

sections.title: A conversation does not tell you what was promised
sections.lede: Ask a Slack workspace what is outstanding for a client and the answer lives in someone’s memory, or in whichever tracker you bought and now maintain alongside it. Kolabr answers in the channel: any message becomes a numbered request with a category, an owner, a due date and a response target the client can see.

cards.title: One subscription, not three
cards.body: Chat, requests, wiki and scheduled events are the same product. Nothing to integrate, nothing else to renew in March.

cards.title: The client sees the clock
cards.body: Response targets are visible to the people waiting, which is why they stop phoning to ask where something is.

cards.title: Nothing scrolls away
cards.body: A promise becomes a numbered request instead of a message that was true last Tuesday and is now four thousand lines up. How that client’s work is actually done is written up once on the channel’s wiki.

outcome.title: What changes in the first month
outcome.lede: Not a list of features. Four things that are different about your week, rather than different about the software.

items.lead: You stop choosing who to invite
items.text: The question “is this person worth a seat” disappears, because the answer is always no charge. The people who actually have the questions are in the room, and the relaying stops.

items.lead: Nothing is outstanding without an owner
items.text: Every promise made in the chat carries a number, a name and a date, and the client can read all three without asking you for an update.

items.lead: The same answer stops being typed twice
items.text: Scope, process and the quirks of that account go on the channel’s wiki once, so a new starter and a new client contact read it instead of asking you.
Chat, requests, the wiki and scheduled events come off one invoice, so the tracker and the knowledge base you were paying for alongside Slack come out of the budget.

items.title: Are Slack guests free?
items.body: A single-channel guest is free, and you may have up to five of them for every paid active member. The moment that person needs a second channel they become a multi-channel guest and are billed at your full per-seat rate. So the honest answer is that guests are free while one channel is genuinely enough. In Kolabr a guest is free in any number of channels, with no allowance to count and no upgrade to trip over.

items.title: What is the difference between Slack Connect and a guest?
items.body: Slack Connect shares a channel between two Slack workspaces, so each person stays in their own account under their own policies. For shared channels both organisations need a paid Slack plan; one-to-one messages work on any plan. A client on Slack's free plan, or not on Slack at all, falls back to being a guest in your workspace. Kolabr has no such condition: a guest only needs an email address.

items.title: Is Kolabr cheaper than Slack?
items.body: Usually, and by a lot once your clients need more than one channel. Twelve people with eight clients of five each, every client in more than one channel, is $120 a month on Kolabr Pro and $455 on Slack Pro. For a small team whose clients each stay in one channel, Slack can come out a few dollars less, because one-channel guests are free there up to five per paid member. What the difference buys on Kolabr is requests with owners and response targets, a wiki in every channel, playbooks and scheduled events, which on Slack you build from Lists, canvases and workflows, or buy as another tool.

items.title: Can Kolabr replace Slack entirely?
items.body: Yes, and most customers end up there. Kolabr runs internal team channels, private and group messages, calls and file sharing the same way it runs client channels. What it adds is the layer Slack leaves to other products: requests with owners and deadlines, a wiki in each channel, and scheduled events tied to the work they belong to. Every paid account also gets a Team channel, there from the first day and the one channel a guest cannot be added to, so the internal conversation has a home that is structurally private.

items.title: Doesn't Slack have Lists, canvases and huddles now?
items.body: It does, and they are good. Lists track items with an assignee and a due date, canvases are documents you can pin to a channel, and huddles are calls. What Kolabr adds is the structure around client work: requests with categories, routing and response targets the client can see, a wiki that suggests the right article while someone is asking, meetings and dates linked to the request they belong to, and guests who are free in every channel. In Slack you assemble that from the pieces and keep it working. In Kolabr it is how a channel works from the first day.

items.title: We already have years of history in Slack. What happens to it?
items.body: Export it and keep it. Kolabr does not require you to move history to start, because the usual first step is a single client channel running alongside what you already have. Most teams find the archive matters less than they expected once the current work has one home. The channel you open this week is the one you will be searching next year.

proof.title: Proof takes one week
proof.lede: Pick your most demanding client. Nothing has to be moved, announced or exported for this to tell you the truth.

steps.text: Open one channel and invite the client’s whole team, not just your usual contact. Guests cost nothing, so there is no list to approve first.
The questions are arriving from the people who actually have them, and every promise made in the channel has an owner and a date on it.
You will know from the client, not from us, whether the channel earned its place. That is the only test this page is asking you to run.

cta.title: Invite the whole client, not one contact.
cta.body: Free for one channel, no card. Seven days on Pro or Business when you want the rest. Put one client in a channel and add everyone who matters, because it costs nothing.
